# From an area to composites

This page takes an area of interest (AOI) all the way to composites on the
MGRS grid squares that cover it: search, download, process, and compose each
square. s1bursts provides each of these steps; the loop that joins them is
yours to write, and there are two ways to order it.

| Order | Searches | Processing | UTM zones |
|---|---|---|---|
| [AOI first](#aoi-first) | One for the whole AOI | One batch, with SNAP processes in parallel | All squares must share one |
| [One zone at a time](#one-zone-at-a-time) | One per UTM zone | One batch per zone | Any number |
| [Square first](#square-first) | One per square | One small batch per square | Any number |

Start with the AOI first. When the AOI spans several UTM zones, run it once
per zone. Loop over the squares first when even one zone is too large for one
search.

## Set up

Both orders start from the same objects. `MGRSGrid` lists the 10 km grid
squares that the AOI touches, each as an `MGRSGeoBox`. Its `resolution` is the
pixel size of the composites, so it must equal the `grid_spacing` of the
products:

```{.python}
import shapely
from shapely.geometry import box
from s1bursts import (
    BurstCatalog, BurstProcessor, FileManager, MGRSGrid, ResolutionWeighter,
    RTCConfig, SearchQuery, TimeRange,
)

fm = FileManager("data")
catalog = BurstCatalog(fm)
processor = BurstProcessor(fm)
weighter = ResolutionWeighter(fm)

aoi = box(7.03, 46.06, 7.12, 46.14)
window = TimeRange("2025-08-01", "2025-08-31")
config = RTCConfig(grid_spacing=20)
squares = list(MGRSGrid(aoi, resolution=config.grid_spacing))
search_area = shapely.union_all([box(*square.geographic_extent.boundingbox) for square in squares])
```

`MGRSGrid` includes every square that the AOI touches, whole, and each
composite covers its whole square. So search the squares rather than the AOI:
a burst that reaches only the part of an edge square outside the AOI would
otherwise not be found, and that square would be composed from fewer inputs
without a warning. A later run would then skip the incomplete composite as
finished.

`search_area` joins the bounding boxes of the squares in longitude and
latitude. The catalog rejects a square's exact outline, which has hundreds of
vertices, with HTTP 414, and a bounding box is slightly larger than its square,
so no burst is missed. `intersecting()` later keeps exactly the bursts that
reach each square.

## Why the products take the square's zone

A composite is written on its grid square's pixel grid, in the square's UTM
zone, `square.crs`. It accepts only products on that same grid, so the
products must be processed with `crs=square.crs`. A product in another zone
is rejected when it is composed.

That is why these loops pass a zone and not `crs="auto"`. `"auto"` projects
each burst in the zone that holds its center. A burst spans about 85 km across
the track, so near a zone boundary its center can lie in the neighboring
zone, and its product would then be rejected by the square it was processed
for.

Near a zone boundary, `MGRSGrid` returns squares from both zones over the same
ground, since each zone is gridded on its own. `box(5.9, 46.0, 6.1, 46.1)`, for
example, gives four squares in zone 31, among them 31TGL29, and four in zone
32, among them 32TKR69, which covers half of 31TGL29. Every loop on this page
composes all of them, so that ground gets one composite in each zone. Keep the
squares of one zone if you need only one.

## AOI first

Search the whole AOI once, download and process every burst in one batch, and
then compose each square from the products that reach it. One batch lets SNAP
process several bursts in parallel; see
[Run several jobs at once](processing.qmd#run-several-jobs-at-once).

One batch has one `crs`, so this order needs all squares in one UTM zone.
Check that, and use the zone of the squares as `crs`:

```{.python}
zones = {square.crs for square in squares}
if len(zones) > 1:
    raise ValueError(f"The AOI spans {len(zones)} UTM zones; run the loop once per zone.")
crs = squares[0].crs

bursts = catalog.search(SearchQuery(time_range=window, intersects=search_area, polarization="VV"))
catalog.download(bursts).raise_on_failure()
rtc = processor.create_backscatter(bursts, crs=crs, config=config).raise_on_failure().products
```

Each square needs only the products whose bursts reach it.
`intersecting()` selects those bursts from the search result, and a product
belongs to a burst footprint by its `burst_id` and `sub_swath`:

```{.python}
for square in squares:
    footprints = {(b.burst_id, b.sub_swath) for b in bursts.intersecting(square)}
    square_rtc = [p for p in rtc if (p.burst_id, p.sub_swath) in footprints]
    weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(square_rtc, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window)
```

Passing every product to every square would give the same composites, since a
product that misses the square contributes nothing. Selecting them first saves
reading each product once per square.

## One zone at a time

An AOI across a zone boundary needs one `crs` per zone. Group the squares by
their zone and run the AOI-first loop once for each group. Each zone still gets
one search and one batch, so SNAP keeps processing in parallel:

```{.python}
from collections import defaultdict

zones = defaultdict(list)
for square in squares:
    zones[square.crs].append(square)

for crs, zone_squares in zones.items():
    zone_area = shapely.union_all([box(*s.geographic_extent.boundingbox) for s in zone_squares])
    bursts = catalog.search(SearchQuery(time_range=window, intersects=zone_area, polarization="VV"))
    catalog.download(bursts).raise_on_failure()
    rtc = processor.create_backscatter(bursts, crs=crs, config=config).raise_on_failure().products
    for square in zone_squares:
        footprints = {(b.burst_id, b.sub_swath) for b in bursts.intersecting(square)}
        square_rtc = [p for p in rtc if (p.burst_id, p.sub_swath) in footprints]
        weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(square_rtc, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window)
```

A burst near the boundary is found by both searches. It is downloaded once,
and processed once per zone.

## Square first

Loop over the squares, and run the whole chain for each one: search with the
square's bounding box, keep the bursts that reach the square, download,
process in the square's zone, and compose:

```{.python}
for square in squares:
    bursts = catalog.search(SearchQuery(
        time_range=window, intersects=box(*square.geographic_extent.boundingbox),
        polarization="VV",
    )).intersecting(square)
    catalog.download(bursts).raise_on_failure()
    summary = processor.create_backscatter(bursts, crs=square.crs, config=config)
    rtc = summary.raise_on_failure().products
    weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(rtc, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window)
```

Each search stays small, and each square can lie in another zone. Neighboring
squares share most of their bursts, but each burst is downloaded and processed
only once per zone: the later squares find its files and skip them. The price
is parallelism, because each batch hands SNAP only the few bursts not processed
yet.

## Add coherence

Coherence follows the same pattern, with pairs instead of bursts. A pair that
starts at the end of the window ends after it, so search beyond the window by
the baseline, and keep the bursts and the pairs that start within it. The RTC
products of the same dates supply the weights:

```{.python}
from datetime import timedelta

from s1bursts import CoherenceConfig

found = catalog.search(SearchQuery(
    time_range=TimeRange(window.start, window.end + timedelta(days=12)),
    intersects=search_area, polarization="VV",
))
bursts = found.within(window)
pairs = found.find_pairs(baseline=12).starting_within(window)
catalog.download([*bursts, *pairs.unpair()]).raise_on_failure()

rtc = processor.create_backscatter(bursts, crs=crs, config=config).raise_on_failure().products
coh = processor.create_coherences(
    pairs, crs=crs, config=CoherenceConfig(grid_spacing=config.grid_spacing),
).raise_on_failure().products

for square in squares:
    footprints = {(b.burst_id, b.sub_swath) for b in bursts.intersecting(square)}
    square_rtc = [p for p in rtc if (p.burst_id, p.sub_swath) in footprints]
    square_coh = [p for p in coh if (p.burst_id, p.sub_swath) in footprints]
    weighter.compose_coherence_lrw(square_coh, square_rtc, square, time_range=window)
```

For both polarizations, run the loop once with `polarization="VV"` and once
with `"VH"`: a composite holds one polarization.

## Keep going past a failing square

A square can fail for reasons of its own data. A square on the edge of the AOI
may be reached by no burst at all, so it has no products, and an empty list is
a wrong call that raises a `ValueError`; skip such a square. A burst footprint
can also touch a square without a valid pixel in it, which raises an
`EmptyCompositeError`. Errors like this one are a `CompositeError`, so a loop
can record them and continue with the next square:

```{.python}
from s1bursts.errors import CompositeError

failed = {}
for square in squares:
    footprints = {(b.burst_id, b.sub_swath) for b in bursts.intersecting(square)}
    square_rtc = [p for p in rtc if (p.burst_id, p.sub_swath) in footprints]
    if not square_rtc:
        continue  # no burst reaches the square
    try:
        weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(square_rtc, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window)
    except CompositeError as error:
        failed[square.mgrs_code] = error
```

A wrong call raises a `ValueError` instead, and a composite on disk made with
other settings raises a `ProductSettingsMismatchError`. Neither is a
`CompositeError`, so both stop the loop, since every other square would meet
them too. The [API reference](../reference/index.qmd#results-and-errors) lists
the errors.

Rerunning any of these loops is cheap. Downloads, products and composites that exist
are skipped, so after a failure only the missing pieces are made.
